job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Emeka Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior underwriting analyst at Northgate Mutual, an insurer in Nottingham. I work out what small shops and workshops should pay for cover, based on their premises, their stock and their claims history. I joined in September after my finance degree. I rent a two-bed with a mate from church, and on Saturdays I coach under-tens football.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's tiring?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the bit where a broker rings up and I get to say yes or no, because it feels like a real decision. What tires me is the pile of forms behind each one, and the training days where we sit through slides. My fiancée, Ada, is a primary teacher, and we're planning a wedding for next summer. My dad, a pharmacist, has said he'll help with the deposit for our first place, so money isn't the worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I knew it, the hype always runs ahead of the real thing. At work I'd tell my team the tools are useful for forms and not much else. I'd say to my mates at the football that I'm glad we can all get on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means a steady job and a straight path. I'm learning from my manager, Pauline, who's twenty years in, and I'd be promoted to full underwriter in three or four years. Nottingham has lots of insurance and finance jobs, and I've got over six months saved. I'm happy with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, take my CII exams, which are the insurance qualification, and keep using the AI helper for first drafts of policy wording. I'd save for the wedding and the deposit, about £600 a month together. And I'd keep coaching on Saturdays, because that's the thing I really enjoy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I like it when the road ahead is clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI tools now and then. What for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it to tidy the notes I write after a call and to explain odd terms in a policy. I take what it gives me with a pinch of salt, because it once invented a clause. So it's a helper, not a boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still weigh on you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding costs, honestly, and prices going up. Ada and I want a house within five years, and rates and prices are against us. That would be the same whether or not AI does anything.

say: I'd say the **hype** always runs ahead of the real thing.
I'd tell my team the tools are good for **forms** and not much else.
think: It means a **steady job** and a straight path, with promotion in three or four years.
Nottingham has lots of **insurance** jobs, and I have savings.
do: Take my **CII exams**, the insurance qualification.
Keep using the AI helper for **first drafts** of policy wording.
Save about **£600 a month** for the wedding and the deposit.
feel: I feel **calm**, because I like it when the road ahead is clear.
S0.quote: I take what it gives me with a pinch of salt, because it once invented a clause.
fieldNote: Emeka is **secure**, with a clear promotion path and local jobs.
His AI use is **cautious**, shaped by one invented clause.
The real pressure is the **wedding and house**, not technology.

steps.text: Take the CII insurance exams on schedule
Use the AI helper for first drafts of policy wording
Save £600 a month for the wedding and deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real and it's coming, and we should make the most of it. I'd say to the team that we should train properly and share the benefit with customers. And I'd say to my dad that businesses will adapt, because they always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, a lot of my job is the standard cases, and those are what the card talks about: checking, deciding on routine risks, answering brokers. A tool can read a proposal form and price the standard ones. That leaves the odd ones for people, but Northgate would need fewer of us. I'm one of the newest, so I'd feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start by learning the underwriting tool properly, not just the odd email. I'd ask Pauline to put me on the tricky cases, like workshops and landlords with strange histories. I'd save more, about £800 a month, and I'd keep the wedding plans modest, so we're not trapped by costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but still hopeful. I've always believed that if you work hard and keep learning, it works out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Underwriting involves checking and deciding. Which part would a tool take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The standard small-shop policies go first, the ones with clean forms. The odd, messy ones stay with humans for a while, because brokers like talking to someone they trust. If I can be the person who handles the messy ones, I'll be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Pauline's job change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pauline would be managing the tool and checking its work, which is a good job. She might get a smaller team. I'd want to learn her job, because it's what I'm aiming for anyway.

say: I'd say it's real, and we should **train properly** and share the benefit.
I'd say businesses will **adapt**, as they always have.
think: Many of my cases are **standard**, and a tool can read the form and price them.
Northgate may need **fewer** of us, and I'm one of the newest.
do: Ask Pauline to put me on the **tricky cases**.
Save **£800** a month and keep the wedding modest.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, but hopeful that hard work and learning still pay.
S1.quote: If I can be the person who handles the messy ones, I'll be fine.
fieldNote: Emeka sees himself in the **standard cases** and responds by aiming for harder ones.
He plans **modest** wedding costs, a practical tie between family and work.
His optimism is **learned**, from his family.

steps.text: Learn the underwriting tool properly, beyond emails
Ask Pauline for the tricky cases

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and nobody should pretend otherwise. I'd say families and churches have to be ready to help, and employers have to be honest. I'd say it plainly, because that's what a man should do, tell the truth to those around him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Private view: my job is probably gone by 2028. Underwriting is judgement on numbers, which is exactly what the card means by thinking work. The robots three years later don't change that, I don't work with my hands. I'd be twenty-four and likely stuck, even with my savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move the wedding forward but make it small, and I'd save everything I could, about £1,000 a month. I'd look at hands-on work that I could train for, like becoming an electrician with my uncle, because that lasts longer. And I'd ask my dad whether he'd still help with a deposit, or whether we should hold the cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, to be honest. Not a feeling I'm used to. I'd try to be strong for Ada and then lie awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What happens to the wedding and the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit her down, tell her plainly, and say that we should decide together. I'd want her to say yes to a small wedding, and I'd tell her I'd take any honest work. She'd probably say we'll manage, because she's strong that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ada?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on the house. A mortgage without a job is a rope round your neck, and I'd rather rent for a few years. But I'd still marry her, because that's the part that matters, and a wedding doesn't need a big venue.

say: I'd say it's too **fast**, and employers must be honest.
I'd say families and churches must be ready to **help**.
think: Privately, my job is probably **gone by 2028**, since underwriting is judgement on numbers.
Even with **savings**, I'd be twenty-four and likely stuck.
do: Move the wedding forward but make it **small**.
Look at **hands-on** training, like becoming an electrician with my uncle.
feel: I feel **scared**, not used to it, and I'd lie awake after being strong for Ada.
S2.quote: A mortgage without a job is a rope round your neck, and I'd rather rent for a few years.
fieldNote: Emeka expects the job to go and moves to **hands-on** trades.
He protects the **marriage** but delays the house.
His sense of **duty** to tell the truth shows.

steps.text: Hold a small wedding sooner and cut the costs
Save £1,000 a month while the job lasts
Ask my uncle about electrician training
Hold off buying a house and keep renting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's time to plan carefully. Firms and churches should help people retrain, and young people should be encouraged to learn trades and skills. I'd say it with some confidence, because five years is enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have five years of work and be twenty-seven by then, maybe a full underwriter. That's a decent runway. I'd still expect my desk job to go, so I'd plan the next step properly, maybe running my own small insurance broker's office, which needs trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my CII, which helps for broking. I'd use the AI tools well, since I'd run a small shop with them. I'd marry Ada, buy a small house with my dad's help in two years, and keep the rest in savings. I'd also learn how to deal with customers face to face, because that's the part tools can't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better, hopeful even. Five years feels like a decent season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years is longer. What do you do differently from the two-year answer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably for the first years, and then I'd leave to run a small broker's shop. Brokers sit between customers and insurers, and people like a face they trust. If there's work for a person in the whole chain, it's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in insurance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be firefighting. With five I'd get married, buy the house and plan the broker idea. I'd rather build than react, and five years gives me room to do that.

say: I'd say it's time to plan **carefully**, with firms and churches helping people retrain.
I'd encourage young people to learn **trades and skills**.
think: I'd be twenty-seven, maybe a full **underwriter**, with a decent runway.
I'd still expect my **desk job** to go, so I'd plan the next step.
do: Finish my **CII** exams, which also help for broking.
Marry Ada and buy a small **house** within two years.
Plan a small **broker's office** that runs on trust.
feel: I feel **hopeful**, as five years feels like a decent season.
S3.quote: I'd rather build than react, and five years gives me room to do that.
fieldNote: Emeka picks **broking** as a human-trust route and wants to own a small business.

steps.text: Finish the CII exams, which also help for broking

Plan a small broker's office to open around 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a blessing, and we should use it to build things that last. I'd say that businesses should keep training young people and that families should teach their children to work. I'd say it from the heart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's very manageable. By 2036 I'd be thirty-two, with children, a house and maybe my own firm. The thinking work would be done by machines, but I'd have a trade I built myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work and build my career. I'd marry Ada, buy a house, save into a pension, and probably open my own broker's office around year five. I'd use AI tools heavily in that, since it's what lets a small shop compete. And I'd keep up the football coaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I think this is how most people would like change to come, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is long. What would you be doing in year four?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year four I'd be running a small broker with two staff, a toddler at home and Ada pregnant, I hope. I'd be paying down a mortgage, going to church and coaching football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want to say to your children, if you have them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to work hard and be honest. I'd tell them machines will do many things, but trust is something only people can give. And I'd tell them not to be afraid of learning, because the people who kept learning were fine.

I'd say businesses should keep **training** young people.
think: For me it's very **manageable**, and by 2036 I'd have children and a house.
The thinking work would be done by machines, but I'd have a **trade** I built.

feel: I feel **calm**, since this is how I'd like change to come, slowly.
S4.quote: Machines will do many things, but trust is something only people can give.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the house and wedding plans would both be under pressure and I wouldn't have time to turn myself into something new. What would help is employers being honest early, training that leads to a real job, and our church and families staying close.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I've always been told hard work pays, and I believe it, but I'm not sure that holds when a machine can work harder. I'd like to hear a better answer than the one I've got.

headlineQuote: I've always been told hard work pays, and I believe it, but I'm not sure that holds when a machine can work harder.
portrait: Emeka, 22, is a **junior underwriting analyst** at an insurer in Nottingham, and uses AI tools now and then.
He is traditional, churchgoing and engaged, and wants a **wedding, house, family**.
He expects standard cases to go first and aims to handle **messy cases** or run a small broker's shop.
His mood runs from calm to **alarmed** at two years, and he protects the marriage first.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because the house and wedding would be under pressure with no time to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: Employers being **honest** early, and training that leads to a real job.
